title: The farewell sermon, again
hook: lives sacred, women honored, all from Adam, read now as a whole
tomorrow: what should a new leader say on day one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, noble character: answer a wrong with better. That was one man's prayer. Today, a crowd, and the Prophet's last pilgrimage.

Comment sections sort people fast: where you're from, how you look, which accent you have. A speech long ago went the other way. On his last pilgrimage, before the gathered pilgrims, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, spoke of lives as sacred, of women as owed their rights, and of everyone as children of Adam. This path has met it before. Today, read it again, whole, and hear two ways Muslims read it.
screen: `SORTED BY ACCENT AND ORIGIN.` → `A SPEECH THAT WENT THE OTHER WAY.` → `TWO WAYS TO READ IT.`

segments.voice: The sermon isn't one document. Its lines are kept in several reports. In al-Bukhari, the Prophet says your blood, your property and your honor are sacred to one another, as sacred as this day, this month, this town. In Muslim, he says to fear God concerning women, and that they have rights over you. And in the Musnad of Ahmad: your Lord is one and your father is one; no Arab is better than a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab than an Arab, nor red over black, nor black over red, except by piety. Now, two readings. Some teachers gather these into one speech and read it whole: sacred blood, women's rights and one father hold each other up, a single picture of human worth. Others read each report on its own chain: the strongest lines stand firmest, and the gathered speech stays a gathering, not a recording. One side guards the meaning; the other guards the exact words. And both arrive at the same line, because the Qur'an says it too, in Pickthall: “O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another.”
screen: `ONE SERMON, SEVERAL REPORTS.` · `SACRED LIVES, WOMEN'S RIGHTS.` · `READ IT WHOLE, OR REPORT BY REPORT.` · `NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW.` · then, large: `ALL FROM ADAM.`

segments.voice: Read the Qur'an's line slowly, out loud if you can: made male and female, made nations and tribes, that you may know one another. Pause after each phrase. Let one face come to mind, someone from a nation or a tribe that isn't yours, and stay with that face until the bell.
screen: `READ IT SLOWLY, OUT LOUD.` · `ONE FACE, NOT FROM YOUR TRIBE.`

howItsDone: Muslims hear the farewell sermon retold in Friday sermons and classes; teachers read it both as one gathered speech and report by report, with Qur'an 49:13 alongside.

fork.setup: your study group splits: one friend reads the farewell sermon as one speech; the other checks each report's chain. you're asked for the second friend's best case. which is it?
options: exactness guards the Prophet's words: the strongest reports stand firmest.
the sermon is probably invented, so none of it should be trusted.
reading it whole is wrong because it waters the message down.
fork.reveal: the careful reading throws nothing out; it weighs each report so the exact words are kept. the whole reading guards the meaning. both are protecting the same words.
